title: The Niagara Commission rejected every plan, pneumatic ones included
detail: In 1890-91 the International Niagara Commission, headed by Lord Kelvin, reviewed schemes ranging from pneumatic pressure to ropes, springs and pulleys, plus direct current. It rejected them all, and Westinghouse won the alternating-current contract in late 1893.
why: PBS says this almost word for word, and a search on Oct. 5 agreed.

title: City-scale water and air power worked
detail: London Hydraulic Power, founded in 1883, ran about 180 miles of 800 psi water mains until its last pump house closed in 1977, driving lifts, cranes and theater stages. Paris pushed compressed air through street mains, first to run its clocks.
why: A search on Oct. 5 agreed on London’s numbers. The Paris clocks are in an 1882 magazine article.

detail: Charles Taylor’s hydraulic air compressor at Ragged Chutes, on the Montreal River near Cobalt, Ontario, opened in 1910 and fed compressed air to mines for about 70 years, with almost no moving parts.

title: Love’s Model City became Love Canal
detail: William T. Love proposed a power-canal city in 1893, broke ground in 1894, dug about a mile and lost his investors by 1897. The unfinished ditch became Love Canal.

detail: London put the first traffic signal outside Parliament on December 9, 1868. A gas leak blew it up on January 2, 1869, burning the policeman who ran it, and London’s next signal was an electric one in 1926.

title: Local Niagara stone probably doesn’t swell in concrete
detail: Quarried Niagara Escarpment dolostone isn’t alkali-reactive, so concrete that grows needs imported stone. The classic swelling rock comes from Kingston, Ontario, where the alkali-carbonate reaction was identified in 1957.

detail: Probabilistic record linkage ran on computers by 1959 and got its formal theory in 1969. False matches can merge 2 people into 1 or create a person who never existed.

title: Ethylene ripens everything nearby
detail: Ripening fruit gives off ethylene, and tiny amounts, well under 1 part per million, set off ripening in nearby fruit. Labs could measure it at those levels by the early 1960s.

title: Temperature can do more than I first said
detail: Chemical quality loss speeds up about 2 to 3 times per 10°C. Microbial spoilage near fridge temperatures is more sensitive, often 4 to 10 times per 10°C, so a cold room drifting from 1°C to 8°C could spoil food several times faster.
why: The corpus said temperature alone couldn’t change spoilage much. A search on Oct. 5 turned up Q10 values of 2 to 10 for refrigerated foods, which fits Ratkowsky’s growth model.
check_first: Ratkowsky et al. 1982, Journal of Bacteriology | https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.149.1.1-5.1982
if_wrong: If temperature can’t do it, you’re back to ethylene or atmosphere.

title: A disconnected line can stay on the wire
detail: Phone pairs were wired to appear at several terminals along a cable. When a customer disconnected, the pair stayed in place, still wired to every terminal, and unused branches called bridged taps hung off working lines.
